questions.prompt: What is Taleb mainly testing in this chapter?
choices: Whether all inequality should disappear
Whether hierarchy is joined to shared downside or protected from it
Whether wealth is always immoral

explanation.gentle: The chapter asks whether the powerful share the downside.
explanation.direct: Taleb is testing legitimacy through exposure, not visual equality alone.
explanation.competitive: He wants to know who stays in the blast zone.

questions.prompt: Why can an unequal arrangement still be legitimate in Taleb’s frame?
choices: Because inequality never matters
Because the people with more reward may also carry more risk and consequence
Because winners define justice

explanation.gentle: Shared burden can make unequal roles more coherent.
explanation.direct: Taleb allows for hierarchy when reward and downside remain linked.
explanation.competitive: If the top can still get hit, the ladder changes meaning.

questions.prompt: When does inequality become suspect in this chapter?
choices: When everyone can see it clearly
When gains are privatized and losses are shifted onto others
When success follows effort

explanation.gentle: The problem is protected privilege, not difference alone.
explanation.direct: Transferred downside is what turns hierarchy into suspect asymmetry.
explanation.competitive: Upside upstairs and pain downstairs is the red flag.

questions.prompt: How does Chapter 7 grow out of Chapter 6?
choices: It ignores prestige and focuses only on income
It extends the critique of insulated status into a critique of insulated hierarchy
It abandons the skin-in-the-game principle

explanation.gentle: Chapter 6 questioned prestige without correction; Chapter 7 questions hierarchy without shared downside.
explanation.direct: The same symmetry test is now applied to reward and rank.
explanation.competitive: First prestige floats free, then the ladder does.

questions.prompt: A leader takes a larger share of profits but also personally loses when the enterprise fails. What is the most Taleb-like reading?
choices: The inequality may still be legitimate because downside is shared
The hierarchy is automatically unjust
Profit alone proves corruption

explanation.gentle: Taleb allows for unequal reward when exposure remains real.
explanation.direct: Shared downside gives the hierarchy moral coherence even if it is uneven.
explanation.competitive: The top still belongs to the same fire zone.

questions.prompt: Why is skin in the game a fairness test here?
choices: Because it makes outcomes equal
Because it shows whether the powerful live inside the same reality they impose on others
Because it eliminates competition

explanation.gentle: The key is whether decision-makers share the harms they help create.
explanation.direct: Taleb uses shared exposure to judge legitimacy of rank and reward.
explanation.competitive: If the top floor has a different downside regime, the building is crooked.

questions.prompt: What does Taleb reject in this chapter?
choices: Any form of success
Generic envy-based leveling as the main issue
All leaders and owners

explanation.gentle: The chapter is not mainly about resentment toward difference.
explanation.direct: Taleb targets illegitimate hierarchy, not every unequal outcome.
explanation.competitive: He is anti-rigged elevation, not anti-winner.

questions.prompt: A planner imposes risky changes on a community but does not live with the costs if the changes fail. Why is this suspect in Taleb’s frame?
choices: Because planners should never act
Because authority is detached from the downside it creates
Because communities always resist change

explanation.gentle: The planner is outside the burden structure.
explanation.direct: Legitimacy weakens when the decision-maker is sheltered from the consequences.
explanation.competitive: The architect of the pain lives outside the blueprint.

questions.prompt: What should you ask when looking at an unequal hierarchy, according to this chapter?
choices: Who has the best public image
Whether the people at the top also share the main downside
Whether the rewards look impressive enough

explanation.gentle: Shared downside is the chapter’s main filter.
explanation.direct: The key question is where the burden lands when things go wrong.
explanation.competitive: Ask who still bleeds when the system breaks.

questions.prompt: How does Chapter 7 prepare the move toward Lindy?
choices: By making equality the only trust signal
By sharpening legitimacy tests before the book adds time and endurance as a further filter
By ending the book’s concern with credibility

explanation.gentle: The chapter checks fairness through exposure before the next chapter adds time as another credibility test.
explanation.direct: Taleb moves from burden-sharing to durability as a further way to judge what deserves trust.
explanation.competitive: After the pain audit comes the time audit.
